historical_record.description: A permit was issued to build a small wood-frame chapel, 24 by 36 feet and 20 feet tall at a cost of $900, on this lot for a neighborhood church and Sunday School.
The Presbytery of San Francisco formally recognized St. James Presbyterian Church, then 69 members strong.
A permit was issued for a one-story 25-by-50-foot building behind the chapel, later mapped as a gymnasium.
A two-story 12-by-25-foot addition to the chapel was permitted, with a kitchen, two toilets and a hallway below and two rooms above, the work to be done by church members.
Before the present church went up, the original 1906 chapel was moved off the lot and around the corner onto Schwerin Street, where it became a house.
The new church cost about $9,500, paid by the congregation with a $2,800 grant from the Presbyterian Board of National Missions.
A permit was issued to add a dressing room and showers to the rear gymnasium building.
Julia Morgan completed plans for the church, a T-shaped two-story frame building with a Sunday School below and the sanctuary above.
A permit was issued for a 48-by-56-foot, two-story wood-frame church on a concrete foundation, clad in stucco and rustic siding.
A construction trade journal announced that Julia Morgan had won the design of a two-story-and-basement frame church for the congregation.

In place of the rose and arched windows Morgan drew, the facade received a stained-glass window of the Parable of the Sower, made by Campbell Glass and Paint Co. of Kansas City and, by congregation lore, salvaged from a church in a Nevada ghost town.
The new church building was dedicated.
By 1938 the 1908 rear gymnasium building had been cleared, leaving the back of the lot empty.
With the Sunday School crowded, the congregation began planning a rear addition.
A permit was issued for a rear addition of 1,292 square feet upstairs and 960 downstairs, holding a small chapel and four classrooms and shortening the sanctuary by about one bay.
The kitchen was remodelled.
The sanctuary received its present pews as a gift; several original pews went to the rear chapel.
In the late 1980s the Presbytery of San Francisco reorganized St. James as a mission church and its first Filipino ministry.
The congregation ordained its first Filipino pastor.
The building was re-roofed.
A chair-lift was installed on the stair to the sanctuary.
With membership dwindling, the church chose not to replace its retiring pastor and closed for nearly two years.
The church partly reopened late in the year with a part-time pastor.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 308, St. James Presbyterian Church.

unknowns: The rear building is shown gone by 1938, yet part of it still appears as a shed on the 1950 fire-insurance map.
